I am soriy I did not mention the Greeks. They are doing a wonderful work. Their resistance has been nothing short of a miracle. I know all hon. members hope and pray that that nation will be able to continue to carry on as it has for the past three weeks and repel what is probably the most cowardly assault which has been made during the course of a war remarkable for the cowardice of unwarranted attacks upon small nations.
Canada has a responsibility to bear. We are the senior partner in the commonwealth outside Great Britain. We are not, as was the case in the last war, simply making a contribution to the common pot; we are in the war as a partner. In the particular work with which I am associated for the moment it is patent to all the people of the world that eventual success cannot be won until we first achieve air equality and then gain such air supremacy as will permit us to take the offensive without which no war can be won. In this respect the Dominion of Canada has a far greater responsiblity than was ever dreamed of during the last conflict. We are the mainstay and right arm of Great Britain. In so far as the joint air training scheme is concerned we believe that we have reached the point where we can predict the success of the plan and the attainment of our common object. In order to do this, and I say this frankly without any hesitation at all, we need the help, the advice and the support of every hon. member of the house and of all the people of Canada. I do believe that we will receive it.

The Address-Mr. Gillis

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with
a great deal of interest to the presentations of the different members, and particularly of the ministers who have addressed the house during this debate. I appreciate the difficulties of the ministers charged with the responsibility of the different departments connected with our war effort. The presentation of their reports to the house was a job in itself. I am afraid that throughout the country' they are not receiving the cooperation that they should. As a member representing a Nova Scotia constituency I am pleased to see on the other side of the house the former premier of Nova Scotia who is now Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs (Mr. Macdonald). While I know we will disagree on many subjects during the time we are privileged to be here, I believe I am safe in saying that in the matter of seeking a solution for the problems of Nova Scotia we will have no trouble in getting together.
I should like to make a brief reference to two statements which were made in the house by the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). I do not intend to take up the time of the house in discussing controversial matters that may not amount to very much, but I should like to direct attention to the fact that with the situation as it is, both in Europe and in this country, the two hon. members referred to, particularly the hon. member for Cochrane, characterized this group as communists, fascists and nazis. Later on, the Minister of Agriculture referred to the philosophy and programme of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation as being state socialism or the state supreme.
As a member of this group I want to make my position clear. I am as much opposed to state-ism as I am to any other "ism." I have absolutely no intention of accepting a dictatorship in any form. I want to make that clear. My conception of the programme and philosophy of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation is that they are the same as the programme and philosophy of the British Labour party. They conform in practically every detail with those of the present government of New Zealand. I do not think either the British Labour party or the government of New Zealand can be characterized as being communistic or fascist, or as adhering to any other form of "ism." I consider them as being forms of straight democratic government. They are carrying on the prose-;ution of this war in every way possible and with a vifew to utilizing the resources of the country in the interest of all people and on the basis of human needs.
If the opinions and ideals of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation can be put into operation in the future, I see Canada as being a country where the government would act merely as a board of administration. In my judgment the most important thing in any order of society is the people, and the people should control at all times. Any government that gets too far away from the people will find itself in hot water in a very short time. I make these remarks just in passing because the remarks of the hon. member and the minister have been carried in the press and now appear on Hansard. As a member of this group I do not want to be classified as being one advocating state-ism, the state supreme or the regimentation of our people. Nothing is further from my mind and nothing is further from the policy and the programme of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation as I understand them.
I listened with considerable interest to the different hon. members who have addressed the house. Without exception they all stress the necessity of winning the war, and rightly so. I was struck with the evident sincerity with which they placed their views before the house, but I would caution hon. members that the winning of the war and the preserving of democracy require something more than lip-service. As I understand it, democracy is not a theory, it is a practical working force that gives all people a voice in the management of the affairs of our country and the right to exercise in economic, political and sectarian fields the rights that are inherent in a democratic system. I feel, too, that in Canada we all should share and share alike, we should share that which is good or evil, enjoying the good things of life where we can and sacrificing where we must. I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated the case quite clearly when he referred to labour in his "Let's Face the Facts" broadcast on Labour day. I listened to that speech, and I read it. I think it sets out the cause of labour in a very clear manner. I should like to quote two paragraphs as follows:
In war, no work, no effort, can compare with the sacrifice of the soldier, the sailor and the airman. Their sacrifice is uppermost in the thoughts of this nation; it will live in its memories. But Canadians will remember, too, the debt they owe to labour. In Canada labour has extended its hours, surrendered its holidays and, in its determination to increase and advance production, has taught the young and the inexperienced the intricacies of complicated trades. It will be the duty of the people of Canada, realizing these things now, to remember them in the hour of victory.
My fellow citizens! A distinguished British journalist who recently visited us, said that he found Canada at war with Hitler and at
The Address-Mr. Gillis

peace with herself. We are at war, and we shall remain united in will and purpose. But we can only remain at peace with ourselves if shirking no effort, withholding no wealth, and sparing no sacrifice, we prove ourselves worthy of our two great brotherhoods-the brotherhood of the brave who fight for us, and the brotherhood of labour that works for their victory.	.
As my function in this house is primarily to speak for labour, I question, Mr. Speaker, whether we are proving ourselves worthy of these two great brotherhoods who fight and work for us. Conditions across the country as I have found them certainly cause one to doubt. In the province from which I come, and particularly in the eastern end of it, in Cape Breton island, there is slowly but surely developing among the people a complex that they are not considered a part of Canada. The war has had very little effect on unemployment there and hundreds of young men who have been unable to find employment are trying to get into the army. Petition after petition was read into the records of this house last session, demanding the opening-up of new mines in Nova Scotia. In one section at present there are 127 so-called aliens who have been driven out of employment, and they have 227 dependents. I looked into this question from all angles while the house was in recess, and I found that it was a question not of alienism but of unemployment, the last stand of desperate men to secure employment.
The relief that has been paid to these men is not adequate, and their children are not able to go to school. This question of alienism came up just after Italy entered the war, and while the house was in recess I made it my business to visit that particular colliery to look into this question. I met the miners who were forcing these so-called aliens-they are all Italians-out of that mine. I met the Italians themselves and had a long conference with them. I made it my business to interview the sergeant of the mounted police who had investigated the whole question thoroughly and has a very good grasp of the whole situation. I wanted to find out for myself whether it was really a question of alienism, if the miners were afraid to let these men come into the mines, or whether it was a question of unemployment. My considered opinion is that it is a question of unemployment, and I think 75 per cent of the men would tell you so. Here and there you would meet a man who would say that it was not safe to allow these Italians into the mines.
In that particular section the same thing was tried on two previous occasions. There are approximately 900 men employed in the

mine, and a percentage of them are Italians. But there are also in that section hundreds of young men who have never had a job, and the native miners resent the fact that so many foreigners are gainfully employed while their own young men are walking the streets. As I said before, the same thing was tried on two other occasions, but the union upset it. At the present time the union officials say they are helpless.
We all remember the hysteria that was caused when the Italians entered the war, and in Nova Scotia these Italians were pushed out of their employment. During the last few weeks the union officials made an effort to straighten matters out and have these men reemployed, giving them status as Canadian citizens because, as a matter of fact, they are practically all naturalized citizens of this country and members of the union as well, and the constitution provides that they should be employed until such time as charges are brought against them of having engaged in subversive activities. But there comes a time when men become unreasonable, and after this thing had dragged along for about three months, when the union officials endeavoured to get these men back into the mine the native miners said no. The situation there is tense, and a telegram I received this morning prompted me to raise the question with the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty). The minister says that his department is cognizant of the situation and that they are trying to find a solution. My considered opinion is that if an attempt is made at this time to force these men into the mine there are liable to be serious repercussions, something I should not like to see happen. The whole question needs to be carefully arbitrated. But at the bottom of it all, in my opinion, is the question of unemployment.
The miners' union is an organization that is very reasonable. It has carried on collective bargaining in that section for thirty years and has never had much difficulty in the past in signing contracts. But at the present time there is not a contract signed. They have been juggling for two years with the mine operators, trying to arrive at some agreement on the question of wages. That further accentuates the unrest among the miners. They develop a complex that they are not being recognized, that their union is no longer serving its purpose, and as a result discipline suffers. That is not a good situation, particularly in our present set-up. The union officials and the men who take a leading part in its organization are endeavouring to iron these matters out and are making little progress in the matter of signing the contracts.

The Address-Mr. Gillis
The people of Nova Scotia, the miners, the farmers and the fishermen-and I have been among them-are developing at the present time a complex of " what is the use?" They argue that nothing has been done, that no progress is being made, and unemployment in that section is much worse to-day than it was when the war broke out. Hundreds of young men are leaving school year after year and adding to the ranks of the unemployed. There has been no employment for them for years, and many of them have tried to get into the army but the units are filled up.
I find that Nova Scotia has gone backwards in the last fifty years industrially, and from the point of view of looking after their own needs. I have discussed this matter with men who have been familiar with the situation there for the past fifty years, and I have here a few statistics which, with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read into the record. Fifty years ago Nova Scotia had: The Merchants Bank; the Bank of Nova Scotia; the Halifax Banking Company; the Bank of Yarmouth; the Commercial Bank of Windsor; the Union Bank of Halifax; all organized, owned and directed by Nova Scotians who loaned money for the doing of Nova Scotia business.
Through mergers all these banks and their assets went west to Toronto; and to-day the money is loaned to Ontario industry. Nova Scotia lost its grip on its cash; and those who profited are living on coupon clipping-not on work-producing effort.
When steam supplanted sails, Nova Scotia had: A cotton mill at Halifax and one at Windsor; a paint works at Halifax; three tobacco factories; four or five shoe factories; two soap factories; several woollen mills (one at Mabou, C.B. won prizes at the Paris and Chicago World's Fairs) ; a big cheese factory at Antigonish, which won the prize at the Chicago World's Fair; a condensed milk factory at Truro; all merged out of Nova Scotia.
At Sydney, the home of the steel industry, which has been pap-fed from its birth to date, we have seen: A cement works drift into a merger; a fertilizer plant leave for Ontario; a local company organized to make small articles from steel be encouraged to spend a lot of capital, and then stymied by Ontario control.
We had Shaw and Mason build a foundry and employ a number of men to supply the steel company. Then a change of control that brought in an element connected with a similar foundry up north shifted the orders away and closed up the Shaw and Mason plant.
A big tar and chemical plant is gradually drifting to the upper provinces.
In every instance Cape Breton is being bled by capital and winked at by partisan politicians. The island is rich in pasture land and fodder hills for sheep. There is good grazing for cows and wonderful land for potatoes and small crops. Cape Breton can feed herself. Our fisheries are abundant, including lobsters, cod, herring, mackerel and swordfish, an asset hardly contemplated since the days of the French. Our people have been exploited. Cape Breton has wonderful gypsum deposits but does no manufacturing. We have great forests but no pulp or paper mills; the raw material is sold at mean prices and our timberlands are denuded. There are dozens of unworked coal seams on Boulardrie island, while Canada is importing coal. There is a rich coal field untouched at Port Morien, from the Hardwood Hill outcrops, which could contribute several million tons of good coal every year. Many of our best coal measures are proven on the Loch Lomond hill, 800 feet above sea level, which is able to contribute big coal outputs with free drainage and free ventilation, an ideal set-up for a profitable mining venture.
The answer to our problem in Nova Scotia, under our present order of society, is the creation in that section of the country of some of the war industries that are being established in Canada to-day. We have everything necessary for the manufacture of war material; coal, steel and iron ore. We are pleading for the government to recognize that section as part of the dominion.
The situation at the steel plant in Trenton, Nova Scotia, was such that on September 27, 1910, one of the responsible officials of district No. 26, the international board member, telegraphed the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) asking that the minister use his authority under Bill No. 43, now the National Resources Mobilization Act, to take possession of the properties of the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal company and its subsidiaries in that section. There are 500 men idle in the Eastern Car plants, and the international board member charged that the Trenton company was on a sit-down strike, that nothing was being done to relieve conditions of semistarvation existing there. He also made a direct accusation of sabotage on the part of that company. That statement was made by a responsible union official. I also received demands from the Thorbum area in Nova Scotia to petition the provincial government for the release of the areas on which the Dominion Steel and Coal corporation holds leases, in order that someone might be interested in undertaking some operations there.
The Address-Mr. Gillis

Conditions of that kind, it seems to me, are not in accordance with the pronouncement by the Prime Minister that we must recognize the value of labour in its relation to the war. I said that to make democracy work something more than lip-service was necessary. In travelling through the provinces of Nova Scotia, Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick I find conditions among the common people anything but resembling those which should exist among a free and democratic people.
The matters with which I am endeavouring to deal this afternoon are not products of my own imagination. I receive letters, telegrams and resolutions, by virtue of the fact that over a period of years I have been actively engaged in the trade union movement. These organizations send these matters to me, and I am here merely endeavouring to act as spokesman for those who send me this information. From New Waterford in Cape Breton I received a resolution passed by the town council stating that there are over 350 unemployed men in that town, with no prospect of obtaining work in the coal mines or elsewhere in that district. The council finds it impossible to raise funds for contemplated local improvements which would furnish work for a large number of these men. The council has made every effort, without success, to secure work for these idle men in public and private projects in New Waterford and other places adjacent thereto. In a resolution which I understand has been forwarded to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), they also make the accusation that work on the extensive public works programme in municipal district No. 20 was being distributed by petty politicians on a patronage basis in view of the forthcoming municipal elections.
In New Brunswick, where I visited the mining section of Minto, I found conditions at least fifty years behind the times. For a number of years the miners in that section have been endeavouring to exercise their industrial democracy by establishing a union and having it recognized for the purpose of collective bargaining, against the direct opposition of the operators and with very little cooperation on the part of the provincial government.
During the recess I had an opportunity of visiting some sections of Ontario, and I was particularly interested in the metal miners in the northern part of this province, with whom I discussed their problems. I find that conditions in northern Ontario resemble anything but democracy. In that area there are from forty to forty-five thousand miners who are endeavouring to form a union. The question [Mr. Gfllis.l
of silicosis was brought very sharply to my attention during my visit. As hon. members know, this is a disease prevalent not only among the metal miners of northern Ontario but also among the miners of Nova Scotia. Last session I discussed briefly with the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), when an appropriation was being put through for research work in his department, the question whether it might not be possible to extend that work to take in this disease of silicosis. That appropriation was small, on account of the war, and the minister did not think there was a possibility of the work being extended, but he did suggest that Ontario had carried on a good deal of research work into this question and that this province had considerable data which might be of some value to us in Nova Scotia. I was glad to get that information, because I also had the opinion that Ontario was well advanced in the prevention and care of silicosis.
As I say, I discussed that matter with the miners in the north, but I found that Ontario was in pretty much the same condition as Nova Scotia. My information is that of some 2,200 persons who have applied for compensation under the Ontario regulation, only twenty-two have had their claims recognized, and I do not believe the facilities in this province for determining whether or not a man is afflicted with that disease are any better than those we have in Nova Scotia. If anything, I think perhaps we are a little ahead of Ontario.
There was brought to my attention one particular case which I think is characteristic of the general trend of the authorities in Ontario who are charged with this responsibility. A man by the name of Steve Kostanyk, who for some considerable time has been suffering from silicosis, has been endeavouring to prove his claim to the compensation board. To date he has been unsuccessful. I have here a copy of the will he made, signing over his body to his friend, a man named Nick Rozok, for the purpose of having an autopsy performed in order to prove that he died from this disease. The compensation laws provide that this disease is compensatable, but in all the years that Ontario has had to deal with this question the authorities have not been able to set up proper boards possessing the necessary facilities for determining whether or not a man is suffering from this disease. I think that is a crime and a shame, and it is merely one case I happened to run into.
We have had the same experience in Nova Scotia. A man named Andrews was afflicted

The Address-Mr. Gillis
for several years with this disease and just recently it was made compensatable in the province and brought under the act. He had not proved his claim. The matter was discussed by the board but owing to the fact that the trouble had existed prior to the passing of the act this man did not come under it. He died only a few weeks ago. The claim was being handled by the union when I left. An autopsy was performed on his body, and according to a press clipping from the Sydney Post-Record of November 3 it was definitely established after the autopsy that Andrews had died from silicosis. It would appear to me that matters of this kind, if they are not taken care of under the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities, whether this be due to lack of interest or to a want of knowledge on the part of the provinces, should come under the federal department of health. It should be the prerogative of the federal department to see to it that men who, owing to their occupation, are prone to diseases of this sort are safeguarded, and research work should be carried on. There are approximately 45,000 miners in northern Ontario and 12,000 in Nova Scotia. In neither of these provinces is there any competent authority who can say whether a man is or is not afflicted with this disease. According to the evidence he must die, and his body must be cut up, before it can be ascertained whether he had been suffering from the disease.

It was diagnosed as silicosis, pneumomycosis and other things by several different authorities. My hon. friend is a medical man; I am not, and I am not going to argue with him. I merely state this particular experience, and I suggest that if the same rule were followed by the compensation board and a proper test carried out when men apply for compensation, much of the misery and suffering which exist to-day would be avoided.
I do not elaborate on these matters for the purpose of hearing myself talk. It may be said that these are isolated cases, but they are not. As I have said, there are
12,000	miners in Nova Scotia and 45,000 in northern Ontario. These men all go down mines and are subject to the disease. They may contract it sooner or later; something that we regard as an isolated condition is a subject of discussion among the men in their unions, and it builds up an antagonism in their minds and the belief that the responsible authorities are not doing what they should do. It was that complex which helped, I believe, to trip up France and the other countries that fell to Hitler.

I believe they are doing the best they can with the machinery at their disposal, but I submit that that machinery should be improved. I suggest that the department of industrial hygiene should carry on research work under the Department of Pensions and National Health. It would be a valuable contribution to the welfare of men employed in the mining industry.
I find that in the Kirkland Lake section, in addition to the problem I have been discussing, a local police force is being set up. In the Kirkland Lake section alone there are 250 men wearing the uniform of policemen and carrying revolvers and batons, and they are drilled by the local chief of police. No one knows what their function is, but I have heard it said among the men themselves, at a meeting I attended, that they bear a close resemblance to Hitler's storm troopers. No one knows exactly what their function is. The miners say that the uniforms are supplied by the local mining companies. During my
The Address-Mr. Gillis

time in a union I have had plenty of experience with company-owned police forces, and I submit that it does not make for democracy in any part of the country to have groups of this sort operating, being responsible to no one that we know of, and allowed to wear uniforms and to arm themselves, for what purpose we do not know. In my opinion, that also creates in the minds of the men in that section the feeling that democratic principles are not being observed so far as they are concerned. That complex is being built up there.
In addition to that, complaints come in by telegram and letter from the Chrysler plant to the effect that workers are not being treated democratically. When they endeavour to follow the principles of democracy the tactics of Hitler are employed by the corporation. When a strike vote was being taken recently in the plant, a number of police officers were stationed outside the union hall at the time the vote was to be taken, soldiers paraded through the plant on the day the vote was taken, and everything possible done to intimidate the men.

I have no doubt the Minister of Labour is correct and I am not questioning what he says. I am, however, not stating my own opinion on these matters; I am simply taking the evidence as I find it. That is the feeling of the men at the Chrysler plant. It was quite a coincidence that on the day on which their vote was being taken, the troops were paraded through. In the opinion of the men everything was done to intimidate them; they felt that it was intimidation. Later on, twentv-four of them were arrested. Some were released, but a few days ago, according to press reports, forty-six more were arrested. If that is the use to which the Defence of Canada regulations are being put, it means that all effective trade union activity in plants engaged in war production will be stopped. If this is the policy of the government, the government must amend its orders so as to safeguard the democratic

rights of the workers to organize and carry on their trade union activities.
Only two months ago the two main organized labour congresses in this country held their annual conferences. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) is a member of one congress and attended its conference; I am a member of the other and was a delegate to it. Both congresses passed resolutions complaining of the treatment of labour in this war, of the fact that labour is not represented on any of the war boards with the exception of the labour supply council which, according to my information, is a dead letter in any event. Organized labour has expressed its readiness, indeed its eagerness to assist the country in the winning of the war in every possible way. The Prime Minister in the passage which I quoted has paid tribute to the workers of this country for their sacrifices. The workers have a right to expect that their needs and their rights will be safeguarded. Their sacrifices entitle them to an equal partnership in the affairs of this dominion, which they can get only through trade union organization and collective bargaining.
Here is what the Monetary Times has to say in an editorial in its issue of November 9, and I do not think the Monetary Times can be characterized as a socialist organ:
The employee, to put it briefly, must first be assured of receiving a square deal; after that government and public opinion may urge fresh sacrifices upon him with a clear conscience.
In all fairness it must be remembered that industry has already been offered fair treatment. No manufacturer has been expected to work on war contracts at a loss to himself. His profit has been assured. These points have been conceded him in advance without argument. The profit motive has been accepted as his proper criterion of when and how much he shall produce. Labour is also primarily in industry for profits and not for glory. Its claims, then, should not be summarily rejected as improper and out of place. No attitude more inimical to the cause of winning the war could be adopted by anyone.
I agree with that opinion. I say that the government should, without delay, implement the policies which are laid down in an order in council relating to labour relations. Of what value is a statement of principle when in practice the machinery of the state and war regulations are used to thwart labour organization and to arrest trade union members?
Complaints also reach us from General Motors in Oshawa that the plant has been placed under the protection of the defence of Canada regulations by a special order in council. It would appear that everything possible is being done for the protection of those exploiting industry for profit.

The Address-Mr. Chambers
It is not my intention in speaking about these things to belittle the efforts of the government. We realize the magnitude of their task in transforming this country from a peace-loving, non-military nation to an effective war-time machine. I fully realize the difficulties, but as one of the men in the street I also recognize the growing danger of allowing the Canadian people to get into the frame of mind that "we have not anything to fight for." At the moment, spokesmen of this country offer the people nothing but a return to the state of affairs which existed before the war. If we continue to do this, the people will not put forward their best war effort.
This generation has been afflicted with two major ware. Before and in between those two wars it has been further tormented by the most complicated economic disorders ever known; actual unemployment or the fear of it have oppressed the spirit of the people during the whole of my lifetime, and its attendant poisons have infected every class in society. No nation "has been immune. In short, the social machinery which men have built up since the beginning of the industrial revolution got out of hand and it came to be realized that the most urgent problem of the day was to bring society once more under control. Men therefore longed for order; for only order could bring security, and for security men have often been prepared to give up freedom. It is in this mood and against this background that fascism makes its fatal, seductive appeal. It says to the tortured soul of Europe, "Give up your freedom and in return we will give you security." We say, "Cling to your freedom." Back comes the question, "What of security?" Men love liberty, but to be free they must live. Old world conditions made the two incompatible. All fascism does is to make the divorce absolute.
We must assure the people of this country a future in which they can be both secure and free. We will fight for it and, if needs be, die for it, but it is not good enough to ask us to fight for the restoration of the old world. It was conditions such as I have attempted to describe that made possible the rise of Hitlerism in Germany and fascism in Italy, and which prepared the way in the countries which have fallen under the nazi heel.

Mr. Speaker, now that I have the honour to be a very junior member of the Canadian Scottish Regiment I feel no diffidence in addressing this house in the French language. I do not need to remind the Frenchspeaking members of this house of the early history of the province of Quebec and of the part played in the development of their beautiful country by people with Scottish blood in their veins. While I was myself not born in Scotland, I am of Scottish descent and the son of a man who fought throughout the last great war in the garb in which I now stand.
During my few short years in Canadian public life I have developed a great respect, may I say an affection for my fellow members who speak the French tongue. Military circumstances will no doubt prevent me from speaking again at this session of parliament and I take this opportunity, therefore, of speaking to my friends through you, Mr. Speaker, poorly no doubt but sincerely, in their own tongue. No one, least of all a Canadian soldier, can gaze dispassionately on the present plight of France. There are some even in Canada who have felt that the French alliance was a misalliance. I am not one of those. I am one who believes in the Entente Cordiale because I have confidence in the French people.
May I take you back, for a few moments, into French history. To the time of the battle of Sedan in the Franco-Prussian war when, as lately, France succumbed before the Hun. Her armies were beaten and scattered and, after a bitter and desperate struggle, the Boche triumphed. But, when the struggle was over, the spirit of France was reborn. The flame in the hearts of a valiant nation was rekindled. The torch dimmed in that struggle burst out again into the flame of Verdun. Through the bitter years of tribute and German domination
The Address-Mr. Chambers

France gathered herself together for the coming fight and when it arrived the people of France conquered.
Let us now, therefore, when we gaze upon the agony of France at this time, remember not that they broke in Luxemburg; remember not that the Maginot line was turned; remember not the incident at Oran; but remember only that history will repeat itself as surely as we are here to-night and that the flame of Verdun will be rekindled when the assault begins.
There are those, too, who have forgotten that France was generous enough to give back the Saar. There are those who say that France should have been more generous. We who live with the oceans on our flanks can never truthfully be the judge of those who live with the enemy as their neighbours. If France has made mistakes let us forgive. Inevitably we, too, have made mistakes. But in the name of the hundreds of thousands of the flower of France who laid down their lives in the last war; in the name too of those scores of thousands of Canadians who lie beside them in the soil of France; let us remember France and let us have faith in the French people.
When I read every day of the deeds of our forces; when I hear from my friends and my relatives in the old land of the civilian defense of our mother country; when I realize from the magnificent figures given to us by those who are charged for the time being with the preparation of our Canadian forces for the assault; I look not backward to the defeat but forward to the struggle and to final victory. I have faith that we Shall conquer as we conquered before-shoulder to shoulder with the soldiers of France.
Mr. Speaker, the traveller who visits the ancient capital of the province of Quebec is told the famous legend relating to an inscription found in ruins of the old city. The inscription of the Golden Dog. The spirit of France, humiliated by German domination, can no doubt be compared to this inscription. When the determination to liberate France will replace the shock of defeat, the nation will arise against its conquerors in the manner predicted by this old inscription:
Je suis un chien qui ronge 1'os En le rongeant, je prends mon repos.
Un jour viendra qui n'est pas venu Ou je mordrai qui m'aura mordu.
(Text) Mr. Speaker, as one who since last addressing this chamber has changed in both appearance and status, I should like if I may for a few minutes this evening to discuss some matters of military moment, rather than those affairs which, were I not in the position in which I find myself, I would have discussed.

Yesterday I listened to the magnificent speech of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), a speech delivered with restraint and full of explanations which hon. members had been seeking.
Since the house last met we on the coast of British Columbia had an opportunity of meeting the minister when he visited the coast. I should like to congratulate him not only upon his speech of yesterday but also upon the fine impression he made upon the people of the coast, and particularly those on Vancouver island. As a member serving in an active service unit I was one of those who in common with many others had to stand inspection. All of us were greatly impressed by the fact that no matter where the minister went, he always had a cheery word for everyone, and nothing was too much trouble for him to inquire into or endeavour to put right.
Also during the recess we had a visit from the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power). His was more in the nature of a flying visit. Then, wC were visited by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs (Mr. Macdonald), who is now member for the constituency of Kingston City. We on the coast were particularly glad to note that the Royal Canadian Navy and its importance in Canadian military affairs generally have been recognized by the naming of a Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs. Many of the people on the island are connected with the Royal Canadian Navy in one way or another, and after hearing and seeing the minister we were all glad that he had been appointed.
Some opinions on military affairs have been expressed in this debate, but I do not propose to comment upon the speeches delivered by other hon. members who are in uniform. Two of the hon. gentlemen who sit on this side of the house and who have spoken are men of much greater military experience than I. Perhaps the sole difference in point of view between them and myself is that I belong to an active service unit. We realize that there have been shortages, but these shortages have been overcome to a great extent by people being willing to put up with them cheerfully as it became necessary.
I should like to comment this evening, from the point of view of the active service force, upon several factors in the military situation. These are matters which I believe might well be discussed in this debate. First of all, there is the question of the training of what will, in the end, be the main fighting force. We have had some thirteen months of war and, as has been stated in the house, we have some 150,000 men in the Canadian

The Address-Mr. Chambers
active service force. During all this period training has been going on. At the outset I should like to say that we are not getting as thorough a training as we should be getting, but we are getting as thorough a training as can possibly be given to us under the circumstances.
I believe that some of these circumstances can be altered. As I said earlier, I have only a limited knowledge of military affairs, but I speak from personal experience and from what I have seen at close quarters. The great need at the present time in the active service force of Canada is that we should be given the benefit of the experience of those who have spent many years in the permanent force of Canada prior to the outbreak of the war. They were learning military ways and making themselves proficient. Many of these men went over with the first or the second division, and a number of them should be brought back to Canada and split up among the active service force battalions in order that the members of those battalions should receive the benefit, not only of what these men have learned during peace time but of what they have undoubtedly experienced in the constant hard training in Great Britain during the time they have been over there. I am not . in a position to know whether these things can be done, but if it is possible to arrange to transfer some of these men from the first and second divisions to active service force battalions in Canada, there is no doubt that in a considerably shorter time than has elapsed since the commencement of training of our active service force battalions they would be in a greater state of proficiency than they now are.
Many of the men in our active service force battalions have been in the army for six, eight or ten months. They are now facing another winter in Canada. Because of our climatic conditions it will be more difficult to train these men during the winter than it would be during the summer months. Now is the time when these instructors, as they might be called, or the more experienced members from the first and second divisions should be brought back to Canada in order to give us the benefit of their training. Those of us who followed developments in the French army from the time of the declaration of war until the attack on the lowlands know what happened because of continued inactivity. I do not want to give the impression that the troops on guard duty on the Pacific coast, such as the unit to which I belong, are inactive. We are anything but. On the other hand, there is monotony to be contended with. Many men who have friends and relatives
in the forces in England have learned many things; they probably know a great deal more than we do, but what we do know is that the monotony of guard duty which has been carried on for nine or ten months and which is likely to be carried on into the winter is not going to make our troops into better fighting men. There will have to be an infusion of new training blood.
Something has been said about the training of those young men mobilized under the national resources act. There has been some debate and discussion as to the length of the training period, and I want to echo what has been said by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks). There is a training camp on Vancouver island and I can say that so far as the training of those men is concerned, it has been a job well done. I cannot say whether the proposal of a four months training period is a sound one. Personally I feel that a period of six or seven weeks would be more to the point. If men are to be trained for four months, it will mean that much of the work which they receive in the early days of the training period will have to be repeated. It may be that you will take the edge off their training and they will probably not be left with a desire to continue their training, as now seems to be the case.
While speaking of training, I should like to point out something of which I am sure the minister is aware. Because of climatic conditions, British Columbia is much more favourable for winter training than certain other parts of Canada. I think this fact should be given consideration by the minister.
Equipment and training going hand in hand as they do, if we cannot have all the equipment we want right off the bat-and one can very easily understand that these things cannot be done overnight-we feel at least that if there were a wider distribution of training equipment among the Canadian active service force units, if that equipment were moved around more than it is at the present time, it would be more beneficial. I do not want to go into a discussion of the training equipment we have on hand or that we have had in our unit, but certainly I should like to see a little more training equipment than we have seen so far, and we hope that it will not be long before we shall do so.
In the minds of a great many of the men serving in the army at the present time there is one unanswered question and that is, how far do the higher military officers in the Canadian forces recognize the difference between conditions in 1914 and in 1940 under which modern land fighting goes on. I put that only as a question. I do not suggest
The Address-Mr. Chambers

that the higher military officers are not apprised of that difference or that they have not a complete idea of exactly what they propose to do and how they are going to do it. But there is in the minds of many of our soldiers that unanswered question, and we are waiting to know what the answer is.
May I say a few words about the soldiers themselves? One thing which has struck me about the present day Canadian active service force soldier is what happened the other day in our own unit, where we have had the ordinary wet canteen right along. We put up a dry canteen and a remarkable thing happened. In about a week's time the wet canteen was doing practically no business at all and the dry canteen was doing it all. That is a change from the last war. I do not know that the example was set by any one of us personally, but nevertheless that is what happened.
It would seem to me from what I know of the men-and the first thing one has to do is to try to get to know the men-is that first of all they know why they are fighting. They are all in the army with a determination. They have a great many suggestions to make, and they make them and we hear them. There is nothing of the automaton either in their actions or in their thinking which heretofore I understand has been a sine qua non of military life. These men have left their homes with a clear idea of why they are fighting and a desire to get on with the job.
I understand that the minister is going to England very soon where no doubt discussions will take place as to the immediate role Canada is to play in the next few months. At some risk of being misunderstood, I would suggest to the minister and the government that he give our men back here at home in the Canadian active service force ranks some hope that they may be led out to do something other than the monotonous tasks they have to perform at the present time. When we see the magnificent defence being put up by England, when we realize that women and children are being killed there and soldiers are not, it makes us feel-I do not know whether I can express it exactly-that we would like to be led out, away from our present humdrum duties, to the job that we joined up to do. But these things are in the hands of those much better informed than I am and in whom I have full faith. You cannot, however, keep young Canadians who have joined to fight, constantly training and training and training and not bring them into action.
The question of war aims has been raised from time to time. I do not know, of course,

what any official statement of our war aims might be, but I think I know from the brief experience I have had with our troops what their war aims are, if one might use that phrase. They want to get a certain job done as rapidly as possible and get back to normal life. They want to know that while they are doing their job, their homes are protected and their families looked after. They want to know, too, that when they come back from that war, if they do come back, there will be as good or a better standard of living for the great masses of the people of Canada.
We understand that the government at the present time has a committee of experts working on post-war plans. I know that suggestions of value have been made to the Department of National Defence in this very regard. It may seem futile to talk now about demobilization, but, Mr. Speaker, you can lay the groundwork for an efficient and speedy demobilization if you do it during war time. One suggestion, for example, that was recently made to the department I should like to see adopted if it can properly be done, and that is that we should have in one compact dossier the civilian labour record of the soldier before he joined up, a record of the training he has taken in his military capacity and its bearing upon future employment, so that when the time comes for that man to be demobilized, the labour exchanges, which I have no doubt will be set up under the unemployment insurance measure, will be furnished with that information, and in particular the office for the district from which the man comes, so that while a job is being sought for him, he can be maintained in the army. That is only a very general suggestion, but I mention it because that information should be assembled now. It is no good setting up boards and commissions to assemble it just when we are going to demobilize our army.
Another matter about which the soldier-I am speaking of the private soldier, is worrying to a certain extent, is the question of insurance. I believe last session the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) brought forward a suggestion in this regard, and I should like to endorse that proposal. I think at this time the government might approach the leading life insurance companies in Canada and ask them as a group, after conferring together, to present to the government, if they feel able to do so, a three-way scheme under which the government might pay a part, the man pay a .part, and the insurance companies take a cut in their rates, thus putting into operation life insurance policies

The Address-Mrs. Nielsen
on behalf of all men serving in the active service forces of this dominion. I do not think that should be impossible.
At the present time, if a soldier wants to insure himself against death overseas, he can do so only by taking out an ordinary insurance policy on which he must pay a very high extra premium per $1,000, I believe somewhere in the neighbourhood of $80. The government might say to these insurance companies, "We would be prepared to open negotiations on the basis of 200,000 men. What rate could you strike lower than that extra $80?" If the premium could be brought down to a more reasonable figure and the difference between the ordinary premium and the coverage for overseas death split between the man and the government, then the scheme might be brought into operation as a voluntary one open to any soldier, any member of the air force or any naval man. I do not know whether that is feasible; I have not had time to look into it, but for what it is worth I offer this suggestion to the government.
Speaking still of the troops themselves, I should like to refer to another question which already has been touched upon, namely, the question of leave and transportation. May I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, in this way; Imagine 300 men on a little neck of land, right on an ocean, fifty miles from the nearest settlement, in a district where it rains all the time. I see the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) giving me a side glance when I say it rains all the time, but in this instance it does. Imagine these men serving night after night, standing guard duty from dusk until dawn, in very heavy rain. Can you imagine how they would look forward to leave, particularly at Christmas time, which leave I now understand has been granted? Then how much more would they look forward to it if, as a Christmas gesture, although perhaps it seems strange to speak of peace and good will in these days, the government gave them transportation to their homes.
Before I finish dealing with this part of my remarks there is perhaps one other group I,might mention. Before this war broke out, a great many of our young men on Vancouver island, who were not at that time being recruited by the Royal Canadian Air Force or the Royal Canadian Navy, left Canada and joined the Royal Air Force or the Royal Navy in England. We have quite a considerable number of young men, Canadian born and bred, serving and fighting in Britain at the present time, who are not actually members of the Canadian services overseas. I believe these young men are not paid as
much for their services as we pay our soldiers, but what I am going to mention comes perhaps a little closer home to the average fighting man. These men of whom I speak do 'not enjoy the privilege of having cigarettes sent to them duty-free, as is the case with Canadians in the active forces. I understand this matter is now receiving consideration on the part of the government. It may not seem extremely important, and perhaps I should not take time to mention it, but it really is important to a large number of young Canadians in England to-day.
I see that my time is very nearly gone. Before sitting down, I wanted, if possible, to tell the house something of the difference in outlook that occurs when one joins the forces. Our spiritual leaders have told us-and I remember an address in the same vein by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King)- that the fight in which we are now engaged is one, to use the words of St. Paul, against spiritual wickedness in high places. Certainly, when one considers the paganism and complete materialism of those forces against which we are struggling, one agrees that in a sense, as the Prime Minister said, the fight is a crusade. I believe, as Cromwell did when he built his new army, that if we have that spiritual confidence, as we have, and combine with it the most modern equipment and the best possible training, there can be no question as to the result. If I had the words I should like to convey to the house something of what that means to the forces. Perhaps I might express that in the words of Rupert Brooke, who said:
Blow, bugles, blow! They brought us, for our dearth,
Holiness, lacked so long, and love, and pain.
Honour has come back, as a king, to earth,
And paid his subjects with a royal wage;
And nobleness walks in our ways again;
And we have come into our heritage.
Mrs. DORISE W. NIELSEN (North Bat-tleford): Mr. Speaker, in looking over the material I thought I might need in speaking this evening, at first I found it a little difficult to decide just which things were of the greatest importance and should be mentioned in the time I have at my disposal. The other evening I listened to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) speak about the problems of agriculture. I listened to him outline what has been done. I also listened to the compliments paid by the Minister of Agriculture to himself. Yet I fail to see what this government is going to do about the wheat situation, especially in Saskatchewan, and it is possible that I should devote some of my time this evening to a discussion of that problem.
The Address-Mrs. Nielsen

With regard to our war effort, it is necessary that this government should take a decided step towards safeguarding the health of our people through the coming years, because every one will agree, I believe, that after the years of suffering which a great number of our people have had to endure, through lack of medical services, through malnutrition and undernourishment, we are going to see a serious loss in working hours if our people do not have some help in that direction on a national scale. Some system of health insurance should be attempted at this time.
There is, however, one subject which is at this time more relevant than any other to the conditions that prevail in Canada, and to this subject I shall give my attention. I refer to the question of democracy itself. We are told that faith without works is of no avail and we also know that ideals, unless they are put into practice, are valueless. Democracy is a way of living, not just an ideal, and so I wish this evening for a while to consider the case for Canadian democracy.
I have listened in this house at various times to tributes that have been paid to the French-speaking people of this nation, tributes in which I have been very much pleased to associate myself, because I know what a great contribution they have made to Canada in the past and I am sure they will make a similar contribution to the history of this country in the future. The other evening I was happy indeed to hear the Minister of Agriculture compliment the English people, particularly since, although Canada is the land of my adoption, England is the land of my birth; and I was more than happy to hear him pay a tribute to the people of London, my old home town. It is in my opinion one of the greatest triumphs of the English people that throughout these last months of terror, throughout this greatest emergency of all times, they have been able to make secure to themselves democracy in England; for no one will deny to-day that the English people have retained the rights and privileges of a democratic people. That has been perhaps their greatest triumph.
It has been said in this house that the first line of our defence is in Britain. I do not remember just which members have said that, but I believe the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) said the same thing only the other day. When I am speaking of the defence of democracy I am inclined to disagree with that opinion, because wherever democracy exists it must be protected and guarded right there. In my opinion the first line of defence of democracy in Canada is here and is now. There is no use in our leaving the first line

of defence to the people of Britain when we are thinking of our democracy; the first line of defence of Canadian democracy must be here in Canada.
Democracy in this country has been built up on the ideals of the two great peoples who constitute our nation, the French and English speaking people. It was, I believe, the great Frenchman Voltaire to whom this remark was attributed: "I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it." That is in essence the very cornerstone of democracy. It is the freedom of speech which is the inherent right of all peoples living in a democratic country.
Besides freedom of speech there is freedom of the press and of assembly; there is the right of every man to be thought innocent until he is proved guilty by a jury of his peers; there is also the right of labour to organize and peacefully to bargain. These various rights have always been acknowledged to be the very bulwark and foundation upon which democracy is built. It is true that we who have watched the growth of fascism in Europe have seen these very things attacked, one after another, by the forces of reaction which have attempted to defeat, and have so successfully defeated, democracy abroad. In Germany and Italy we have seen freedom of speech, freedom of the press and of assembly, the right of working people to organize, all gradually taken away from the people by the powers of dictatorship. Unfortunately, when we come to consider, we find that under the defence of Canada regulations, which we are told are for the protection of the Canadian people against the activities of enemy aliens, certain rights and privileges of people in a democratic nation are also liable to be taken away.
We are at war, and I know it is perfectly necessary in a time of war to do certain things. No one would deny that in a time of war we have to protect lines of transportation and our coast-lines from the activities of enemy aliens. But to anyone who has studied the defence of Canada regulations-and I wish very much that more of our Canadian people would study them-it becomes increasingly clear that although some of our regulation's are decidedly to protect Canadian people from the activities of enemy aliens, there are in the regulations other clauses that are more calculated to defend, from the just criticism of its own people, a government which during the last session took to itself almost dictatorial powers.
It has sometimes been asked; why is it that here in Canada we have not the same freedom of speech which the British people

The Address-Mrs. Nielsen
have still kept to themselves? The reply has been that here in Canada we cannot allow the same freedom of speech because we have certain minority groups. It is true that in this dominion we have people of many nationalities, people who have come from various countries in Europe. They have made a contribution to Canada; they have made a contribution to our living standards, to our thought and culture; and having made that contribution, a contribution of which they may justly be proud, they should be given the full privileges of Canadian citizenship.
To-day we are not allowed freedom of speech because there are certain minority groups in this country, and in my opinion that is an unjust and unfair way of dealing with these people. Many of them have come from countries in Europe where freedom never existed or where dictatorship has gradually taken over and democracy is dead. Many of these so-called foreign speaking peoples are more aware than Canadian-born people of the insidious approach which reaction and dictatorship will make towards the bulwarks and fundamentals of democracy. Many of these people would perhaps warn Canadians of the insidious approach towards the destruction of democracy. I wonder whether it is for that reason that we have lost some-I should say nearly all-of our freedom of speech in this country.
It is also true that in this country a large number of arrests have been made recently under the defence of Canada regulations. This is creating in the minds of Canadian people a great fear as to where our own democracy is bound. I think the majority of hon. members are conversant with the magazine called Saturday Night. In its issue of November 9, Mr. B. K. Sandwell, its editor, has an article which he heads "The Growing Sense of Insecurity. Mr. Sandwell is a man whose conservative opinions and fine sense of values have won him a position of regard in this country. He says:
I doubt whether the government is fully aware of the grave sense of insecurity which is developing among the less influential classes of this country as a result of the workings of the defence of Canada regulations. . . . Canadians have been altogether too lacking in appreciation of the value of the courts and of the prerogative writs as safeguards against arbitrary action, but the present state of affairs is waking them up. Justice, it is true, is never perfect, and liberty can never be absolutely guaranteed to everybody; but the difference between the state of affairs which ordinarily exists in a British country as a result of the ability of the individual to bring his case before an impartial tribunal, and the state of affairs which exists when he is deprived of that ability, is beginning to be appreciated.
According to Mr. SandwelFs report, about 1,500 people have been interned since the defence of Canada regulations came into effect. There are some things I should like to say about the way in which these regulations have been used and the way in which our people are placed in internment eamips. Mr. Sandwell in this article has expressed it perhaps far better than I myself could do, so I wish to continue to quote from his article. He says:
The issue of an internment order which effectually deprives the internee of his liberty even though the confinement to which he is subjected may not be regarded as a punishment, involves no court proceedings, no notice to the person interned, no pleadings of any kind, and no publicity. The police, armed with the order, which has been issued without the knowledge of the person against whom it is directed, simply call for him and take him away. It is often impossible for his family to find out where he is for a considerable time. His neighbours and the press are not encouraged to be inquisitive about him. It has not yet been possible to procure a writ of habeas corpus against the officials who have him in their charge.
Possibly other hon. members have at different times received letters regarding people who have been interned under the defence of Canada regulations. I do not wish to mention many of these cases. One name which I think has received quite an amount of publicity is that of Sullivan, one of the secretaries of the seamen's union; another is a man named Chapman, another named Charles Murray, all union members and working presumably in the interests of the ordinary people. These men have been arrested along with some 1,500 others, according to Mr. Sandwell, under the defence of Canada regulations. I do not know with what these men are charged; I have no more idea than any other person reading of these things of just what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has decided these men are guilty. But the counsel who has been called in for their defence states that these men have been told that representations have been made that they are communists. That may be true; I have no idea whether it is or not. What I wish to ask at this point is, if there are 1,500 people arrested in Canada under these defence of Canada regulations, have they been told what their offence is? They are held in internment camps without trial. If we are to have democracy in practice and not just as an ideal, any man or woman living under British justice should have the right to know what he or she is charged with and to have a trial by jury. If it can be proved that they are members of an illegal organization, all right, let the jury convict them.
The Address-Mrs. Nielsen

But so far as we know, people to-day are being interned in Canada with no right to a hearing and trial before a court and jury.
There is one thing which I believe is left to them; they have the right to appeal to a reviewing committee. Mr. Sandwell in the same article says with regard to these reviewing committees:
There are only two reviewing committees in all Canada, each of them consisting of one person, an English-speaking person being one committee, and a French-speaking person being the other committee. This is not nearly enough to ensure prompt disposal of all the cases demanding review; and a person detained in error or upon insufficient grounds is entitled to prompt disposal of his claim that he is thus detained.
And here is a point which should be impressed upon everyone:
And further-these committees are themselves the sole judge of the amount of information which shall be communicated to the interned person concerning the charge against him; and the amount of information which they are so communicating in some cases is so infinitesimally small as to make defence literally impossible. In one case-
And I believe Mr. Sandwell is referring here to the case of Pat Sullivan.

no more definite particulars of the grounds of detention have been obtainable, despite repeated and formal applications by counsel than that "representations have been made that you are a member of the communist party." All that the detained person can possibly do in answer to these "particulars" is to deny that he is a member. He cannot attack the credibility of the witnesses who made the "representations", for he does not know who they are. He cannot offer any alternative explanation of the acts or events which led to the representations, for he does not know what they are. No court would regard this as an adequate statement of particulars for a moment; but no court has any standing in the matter.
It has always been considered the right of a subject under British democratic rule to be considered innocent until he is proved by trial to be guilty. I feel that in allowing the defence of Canada regulations to be enforced in this manner we are allowing one of the fundamentals of democracy itself to be negated. It matters not to me what these men are or who they are, the fact remains that they are British subjects, and as such they should have the protection of the law which democracy and our British justice have always accorded to us. In this connection I should like to quote also from a man who cannot in any sense of the word be called a defender of the communists. This is Colonel Drew, the leader of the Conservative party in the Ontario provincial legislature. Recently Colonel Drew was speaking before the Electric club at its luncheon in the Royal

York hotel. On that occasion he spoke in defence of democracy, as I am attempting to do at this time. He also mentioned the fact that under the defence of Canada regulations we people are losing some of the essentials and fundamentals which, if once lost, we do not know can ever be regained. Colonel Drew says:
If we are prepared to shed our blood to preserve democracy, we should try to make it work under stress of war.
He goes on to say:
Nobody can accuse me of being a communist sympathizer or enthusiastic about the C.I.O. But the test of a democracy is not whether the people we like are to be protected, but whether the principles of democracy, including public trial, are to be extended to the very limits.
Then he says this:
All these acts are done under order in council, under dictates. Two weeks ago another order in council was passed saying that any article may be destroyed or retained by a justice of the peace at the discretion of the attorney general, whether a person is accused or not. It is said this referred to bombs. But do we need a law to throw a bomb into a lake? It could refer to books and records and documents. It could take from a man, accused or not, the means by which he could defend himself. This is shocking. It offends every principle of British jurisprudence, and it is time we expressed ourselves about regulations of this kind. It is an 800-year old issue, and the question of the right to discuss it is even older.
Also during these last few months we have found that under the defence of Canada regulations certain people have been arrested merely because they have in their possession literature of a certain kind. Yet freedom of the press is another fundamental of democracy. I know many of us have deplored the burning of books in Germany, and we have said that the German people are going back into the dark ages, when they are no longer allowed freedom to read for themselves and form their own opinions.
It is true that we in Canada have not yet reached the stage where we burn books. But we have already come to the point where under the defence of Canada regulations people have been arrested because they have had in their possession certain literature. Recently in British Columbia a bookstore keeper was arrested under the defence of Canada regulations for having books in his bookstore. I cannot help feeling that any intelligent person in Canada must realize that to form an opinion a person must have access to these various ideologies; he must have access to various schools of thought, because it is only by comparison and by contrast that an intelligent person can come to any decision as to what he himself believes. Yet to-day in Canada, under the defence of

The Address-Mrs. Nielsen
Canada regulations, we are having this certain right severely narrowed and limited. This is one other matter which I feel offers a distinct menace to democracy in Canada.
While I am speaking about literature, I should like to mention something else which is perhaps more of a personal nature, but which I feel is something with which every hon. member should be vitally concerned. During the recess reports were brought to me, in my constituency, that the provincial police were going round the country looking for a certain little leaflet I had had printed. It would have been an easy thing for the police, who know me fairly well-I believe I am known to most people in that part of Canada-to come to me and ask for one of those leaflets. I would have given it to them with the greatest pleasure, because it was nothing but an open letter to the Canadian people giving in condensed form what I had said in the debate on the budget. Instead, however, of asking me for a copy, the police travelled miles and miles through the north country, visiting house after house asking for leaflets, and stirring up in the minds of the people fear and apprehension as to what the leaflets contained, and the danger they presented. This is just one example of how the police are operating to-day under the defence of Canada regulations. It is an example of the way in which they are causing fear among our people.
I took great exception to that procedure. On the other hand I saw no reason for undue alarm because, as I have said, the leaflet contained only a condensed version of the speech I had made in the session. I took no action in the matter whatever. It is quite likely that numbers of people, in deference to the wishes of the police, turned in their copies.
I remember that on the first occasion of my speaking in the house I said I would devote my energies and my time, and speak in the interests and on behalf of the life of the Canadian people. I have consistently spoken and written both in and out of this house in the interests of the underprivileged, the inarticulate and the non-influential among our people, and I shall continue to do so. I find that there are others who have said some of the things I have said. I notice that those in charge of the Toronto community chest campaign have published a little leaflet headed with the word " fight." In it they say the same things I have said repeatedly, namely, that we must fight poverty and that we must fight against subversive influences in Canada; that we must fight malnutrition, intolerance, delinquency, distress, despair, unrest, and so on. I note that the governor
general of Canada has said, in connection with the community chests drive, that at this time when our thoughts are on the battlegrounds of Britain we must not forget the righteous claims of our fellow citizens in Canada.
In essence that is what I have always maintained. That is what I have always said to the people in Canada. I find that a little pamphlet like that published by the campaign headquarters is allowed free circulation in Canada. No policeman seeks to blot it out. Why? Because we find that this pamphlet asks for charity. I have never asked for charity for the people of Canada, because I say that is not the solution of their problems.
I have in my hand a pamphlet printed by a newspaper and headed "Democracy must live." It contains a number of the speeches I made in the House of Commons, and also the open letter to the people of Canada, which is nothing but a condensed version of the speech I made in the budget debate. In that speech I did not ask for charity. I said:
We must demand that no person or corporation or institution makes any profit from this war. We must demand that those with great wealth pay the cost of the war and not we who now can only just manage to live.
There is the difference between this pamphlet and the other one. Yet I am informed that the police have been to the offices of the newspaper company which published this pamphlet. I am informed that they have taken the galley-proof and the available copies, and that men in various cities of Canada who have been selling this little pamphlet have been arrested.
