speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do not speak as an
individual. I speak, as do other hon. members, as an elected representative of the people. If democracy is going to live in Canada, then the other members of the House of Commons have the right with me to ask why the voice of one member of the house should be stilled. It becomes increasingly evident that under the defence of Canada regulations anyone may be accused of being subversive if he speaks or acts against the powers that be in this country. If he says anything against the power of finance or against the power of big business, he may be called subversive under the defence of Canada regulations. In Germany, if it were found necessary to discredit anyone or attempt to make everyone take notice, the cry of "Jew, Jew," was raised. In Canada, if certain people feel that they want to discredit anyone, they do not raise the cry of "Jew," they
The Address-Mrs. Nielsen

raise the cry of "red, red." Jew-baiting in Germany, red-baiting in Canada! These are the things I want to bring to the attention of this house. If we have democracy in this country, these conditions must no longer exist.
As I said before, although Canada is the land of my adoption, England is the land of my birth. I have no fear of these things. It matters not to me what I am called. If I am called "red", that does not affect me. Only one thing which would perhaps break my heart is if in this effort to preserve democracy the common people of this country ever had occasion to label me "yellow".
Some of the trade union leaders have also been labeled "red". I do not know whether they are, but if we have any democracy at all we should safeguard the citizens of this country from things of this kind. They should be given a chance in our courts to be proved guilty or to be exonerated from these charges. I was not in the house at the time it was delivered, but I read a speech which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made on September 8, 1939. He made some wonderful statements, and I should like to quote him as follows:
I care not who the individual may be, how respectable in his own eyes or in the eyes of others lie may appear, or what position he may hold; if he seeks to profiteer in this crisis he belongs to the underworld and should be treated as one of those who menace all that is sacred in human relations.
If a man seeks to profit in this crisis, he belongs to the underworld, according to the Prime Minister. There are many people who have been interned because they have worked in the interests of the common people of Canada. Yet we have to-day as members of an advisory committee to this government a number of leading industrialists, men who are bound up with the great financial institutions, industries and big business monopolies. They are members of a committee advising the government on its war effort. Through the corporations which they represent these men are making unprecedented profits out of war contracts. Remembering the words of the Prime Minister, I believe it is also well to remember that this government has as members of an advisory committee men who, according to the words of the Prime Minister, belong to the underworld.
There are no provisions in the defence of Canada regulations to take care of such subversive activities. We should not forget the fate of France. There were those who were guilty of the downfall of that country, those who stole her democracy and relinquished it to the dictators, those who imprisoned thousands of French citizens in

internment camps and prisons, those who set loose the really guilty ones. I think there is considerable need for the Canadian people to see a parallel of these conditions within our own boundaries.
This evening I want to pay a tribute. Many tributes have been paid in this house to the armed forces, and I have joined in those tributes. But I want to pay a tribute to another army, that army of men and women who are without uniforms, who are without ammunition, who have nothing but the courage of their convictions. They have only the ideals of democracy to which they cling, but they are standing in the front line of the defence of democracy here in Canada. These people are to be found in various walks of life; they hold various political opinions and have various creeds. I hope I may be privileged to stand beside those who are standing in the front line in the defence of democracy. These people have done much to help to keep alive the structure and spirit of democracy, as well as the practice of democracy, which matters more than anything else. In closing I should like to quote a few words from the Globe and Mail of October 12, because I believe that in these words is a truth which every Canadian should realize. They are:
It is the unpopular people who are the first victims of any gestapo. The turn of the more reputable citizens comes next, when, after having acquiesced in injustices being done to people they dislike, they find that their own shield against injustice has been destroyed.
I know there are many to-day who feel that those in internment camps are just communists or agitators. They may be, but as Canadian citizens they have the right to a trial and British justice. If we as Canadians are willing to let them suffer without having justice, who knows how many of us will suffer in the same way in the future? It is not only that we have to stand to-day in defence of what democracy remains to us; the Canadian people must gather their forces, and all those who believe in and are willing to defend democracy must attack the powers of reaction which are stealing the very bulwarks of our democracy from us. They must go after the democracy which has been taken away from us. There must be freedom of speech, freedom of assembly and the right to a just trial. Through these years there have been people who have been willing to defend and fight for democracy. If they are willing to give their lives for democracy, then I feel convinced that democracy will never die in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak at this stage of the debate in support of the amendment, I do

The Address-Mr. Perley
so because it provides me with the first opportunity of making a few suggestions to the government and drawing to their attention a matter apart from the war but one which is of urgent importance in western Canada. I think we are all agreed, and it is not necessary to restate it, that Canada's part in this war should be a united one. The day has arrived when petty differences should be set aside. This matter should be looked at from a national viewpoint. I think we all realize that Canada's war effort should be a one hundred per cent effort. May I say here that any achievements or speeding up of our war effort during recent months, such as we have heard of from four members of the government, should not blind us to the fact that our front line is in Britain; or as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) put it, our front line is in the English channel, on the coast-line or wherever Britain desires to lead us in this struggle.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), in his statement to the house the other day, gave us his reason for calling parliament together at this time. He said it was for the purpose of giving to the members first-hand information respecting Canada's war effort and an opportunity to make inquiries after we had heard the statements of the government. I think the Prime Minister realized that the press and the public generally were becoming a little restive and wanted to know. Through parliament we are going to let the public know, and after we have had the full story from the government the opposition will be in a position to decide exactly what we should do. I think it is generally agreed that as an opposition we have the right to make constructive criticisms. I think it is also agreed that we cooperated fully with the government during the 1939 session, and we shall cooperate now if the government shows its desire to have our cooperation by giving parliament all the information it should have.
May I say to the private members supporting the government that they have just as much responsibility as we in the opposition have to see that the government gives parliament the facts, and wherever possible to give the government support in its war effort. We should, however, have first heard from all the ministers, instead of having all this in-between stuff. We should have been given a clear-cut statement of what Britain has asked of Canada. Who knows yet what Britain has asked of Canada? What did Britain ask of us in September, 1939? What did they ask Canada to do in July, 1940? What are they asking Canada to do to-day in the matter of men. armaments, munitions and food? When 14873-13
we have received a clear-cut statement of what Britain is asking us to do, we shall be in a position to judge whether Canada's war effort is the very best of which Canada is capable.
The Prime Minister, in his address to the house the other day, quoted statements that had been made to the British house thanking Canada. That was quite all right. But still we do not know what Britain has asked Canada for. We do not know what they desire as our maximum effort, so to speak, and I think we should be told.
The Prime Minister also mentioned the cost of the war. I do not think this is the stage to go into that because there will be an opportunity to discuss the cost on the budget. To illustrate the seriousness of the war and the great responsibility of the government, the Prime Minister related that at a cabinet meeting one day the government passed war contracts to the amount of $200,000,000, which was quite an order. Here is where the Liberal members sitting behind the government could strengthen its hands if they would only join with the opposition more and insist on a non-political, business-like executive body being set up with authority to direct and coordinate Canada's war supply programme. That is their duty just as much as it is ours. We have boards, missions, commissions and committees, and information is being given to the public with respect to all contracts let, but the volume is so large that I for one cannot begin to analyse or check them, nor do I think any member of the house can. Contracts are being let by the thousand, and we know of sub-contracts being let by the thousand, too, so that it is impossible for us, no matter how much we as members of the house would like to check them, to keep track of them all.
We hear at times of favouritism, patronage and waste. I have heard it from the boys in uniform who have gone from western Canada down east and come back home, and I have heard it from men not in uniform who were employed on construction contracts. These men come back home from time to time and tell of waste and a few other things that are going on which I think should be corrected. I am not going to be too critical of the government or of any minister in that regard, because I do not think it is humanly possible for any minister to keep track of all that goes on.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) and the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) gave us a fair and clear-cut statement of the activities of their departments and showed that they

The Address-Mr. Perley

are anxious to be fair and reasonable in meeting criticism and giving us information. I repeat that I am not charging any minister for some of the things we sometimes hear are going on, for all parties are cursed with a certain class of people who are bound to bring in patronage, favouritism and things of that kind.
One request has been made which I should like to support and that is free transportation and Christmas leave for the soldiers. I do hope the government will take into consideration the suggestions that have been made in that regard. Many of the men are far from their homes and the distance across Canada is great, but I hope the government will do the very best they can and give the boys who are a long way from home a chance to get back for Christmas.
We have heard now from four ministers.
We are all agreed that the war is the paramount question before parliament to-day; nevertheless there are certain domestic problems that are second only in importance to the war, and of such importance that they should be dealt with by parliament now at this session.
We have heard from the Minister of Agriculture. He was the first to go to bat, and his speech may be divided into three parts- introductory; his achievements with respect to the agreements overseas; and thirdly, an account of his trip. I certainly enjoyed listening to his description of what he saw in Britain and his account of the fine spirit of the British people and their firm resolve that they are going to go on until they have won this war. It was splendid to hear the minister describe the spirit of the people he had seen there. I think we were all a little more British after listening to that part of his address.
But I regret exceedingly that in the first part of his speech he ran true to form, just as we have heard from him on former occasions. I say that the first fifteen minutes of his speech was uncalled for, and not becoming to a cabinet minister or one seeking the leadership of a great party. This has happened before; I believe this was the second occasion on which he pulled off the same thing. I do not think the people of Canada appreciate or are looking for that sort of thing at this time. The minister abused the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) and the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell)-

speechtext:
No, they did not look for it. It is their right and privilege to offer constructive criticism. The amendment is

constructive, and the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation also offered constructive suggestions; I venture to say that two-thirds of what he advocated will be adopted by this government within the next eighteen months. I do not think hon. members have to stand for that sort of thing.
The minister went on to refer to the election last March, and cited his own case in particular. I can tell him that if the third candidate had dropped out two days before nomination day, Mrs. Lucas would have been sitting over to my left representing the constituency of Melville. It was the Liberal machine, efficient and well-oiled, that helped to win that election; I might mention such things as dug-outs in his own constituency and telegrams circulated promising bonuses which in some instances never were paid. Just to indicate what really brought about that election result, I should like to refer to the auditor general's report for last year, tabled in this house within the last few days. For the information of all hon. members I should like to quote from page 61 of that report, where the auditor general deals with the administration of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. He says:
Commitments of approximately $1,315,575.20 were incurred in excess of the amount appropriated without certificates of the comptroller of the treasury being secured. . . .
Of that amount the auditor general goes on to say that small projects, such as dug-outs and so on, accounted for S909,553. On the next page he deals with contracts let under this legislation, and says:
The contract with the Northern Wood Preservers, authorized by P.C. 223 of January 31, 1939, provides for the purchase of not less than 400,000 and not more than 500,000 posts. Payments to the company are, by the agreement, to be made after inspection, three cents per post being withheld to secure the subsequent loading. As of March 31, 1940, payments had been made on 494,883 posts-
That was practically the maximum amount authorized.
-but only 188,600 had been delivered.
Then on page 66 we have the report with regard to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, which is the bill under which the bonuses are paid. I should like hon. members to listen carefully to this statement:
Several awards were made by the minister covering yields not accepted by the committee. Farmers were not required to make applications for assistance. . . . Awards have been made on summer-fallow acreage where in many cases the summer-fallow exceeds the seeded acreage. A limited test audit showed that of the total cultivated acreage approximately 35 per cent was in summer-fallow.

The Address-Mr. Perley
And again:
Payments have been made in many cases where the cultivated acreage was too small to put persons in the category of farmers.
And again:
Payments have been made to persons who, in no sense, were grain farmers-[DOT]
That is what has been going on under this branch of the Department of Agriculture. I appeal to hon. members to see to it, when the estimates are under consideration this year, that some direction is given that this sort of thing must stop in Saskatchewan. This is the third auditor general's report to condemn the actions of the minister. I have brought the matter to the attention of the house previously, and I do so again now. This sort of thing should not be permitted, and hon. members are not hon. members if they do not do something to stop it.
The minister stated that the government had spent millions to help the farmers of the west, and mentioned what had been done by way of increasing the storage facilities for grain. I say that assistance should have been given directly to the farmers and not to the grain trade. I should have liked time to recite bow the annexes being built to accommodate twenty-five or thirty thousand bushels will be paid for in three months on the basis of the storage charges being collected. I say these storage charges should be readjusted, because this is very different from grain storage in a regular terminal elevator.
The minister's statement contained nothing definite with respect to wheat, nor did it hold any immediate promise of relief for the wheat grower. As reported at page 101 of Hansard the minister told us what wheat we might expect to sell during the next five years, a total of 2,080,000,000 bushels. This includes 160,000,000 bushels a year to the United Kingdom, 160,000,000 bushels a year to other countries provided the war progresses as he hopes or is over, and 160,000,000 bushels annually for domestic consumption. The last figure is a little high, I am afraid; the domestic consumption at present is only about
110,000,000 bushels annually. I would say the minister is an optimist, but I am going to agree with him in very large measure. I have always been an optimist with respect to our large wheat surplus. I never worried very much about it in Mr. Bennett's time, in 1934 and 1935, when the situation was similar to that which exists at present. I can recall, however, the minister and other members of the house going up and down Saskatchewan at that time saying that Mr. Bennett was hoarding wheat and not selling it, and criticizing us for taking money from 14873-131
the treasury to carry this tremendous load. They also said that Mr. Bennett's policy was one which would bring about the control or restriction of production. Well, I think the minister is pretty nearly right in his estimate;
I think he will get rid of his wheat, but I would like to see him courageous enough to fix the price, as we did under similar circumstances in 1935, at 87i cents.
I am not going to say anything with regard to the control of production. I am a little hesitant about offering any suggestions, because any suggestions I have brought forward on the floor of this house during the last two or three years have been ridiculed by the government, although it is some satisfaction to know that almost all of them have been subsequently embodied in the legislation that has been brought down. If the minister is interested in a proposal I made with regard to the control of production, he might look up Hansard for 1934.
The minister comes to the bouse without anything for the butter producers, although he has something for those producing cheese. What about bacon? Perhaps his statement was a little previous. He spoke of the greater quantity we might ship, but he added, "I cannot divulge the price." Well, it happened that the head of one of the leading Canadian packing plants was in this city, and, I believe, in one of the galleries of this house, the day the minister made his statement, and the price was set the next day. Was that just a coincidence? Why could the minister not have said, "Well, we will have to take a lower price, boys, but you can produce all the pork you like and they will take it." I am afraid there was not very much in his speech for the hog producer. I do not think the minister needed to go to England at all. I believe it would have been sufficient if he had sent the chairman of the bacon board. It seems to me that if the minister's trip cost this country even a dollar, that was one dollar too much, for nothing whatever was accomplished that could not have been accomplished by negotiation with the representatives of the British authorities right here. Let him tell us what he accomplished over there that could not have been achieved by negotiation. He said further that the producers must supply and expect only sufficient to carry on. Let me quote from page 97 of Hansard:
I think it is our duty to place the food supplies available for empire consumption at the disposal of the empire through the food and shipping ministries of Britain, to be directed to any market they think advisable. I think we should receive in return from the British government for these supplies sufficient to make it possible for our farmers to carry on producing food supplies.

The statement is that the farmers are expected to produce as long as they receive sufficient to carry on. May I ask, then, why it is necessary to have the grain exchange remain open? As regards carrying on at cost of production, let me say that our farmers are just as patriotic and are just as much in this war as any other class of industry or any other section of the community, and all we want for them is a fair price, a price comparable with that which industry is receiving for what it produces of the commodities that farmers have to buy.
Take an eight-foot binder. I recall a statement made by the minister last year with regard to the binder used on his own farm. In 1913 it took 260 bushels of wheat to buy that binder; in 1936, since this government took office, an eight-foot binder cost 300 bushels odd; and to-day the same binder costs 630 bushels. What we want is a comparable price, a price that will be fair and equitable, so that all classes will be making about the same sacrifice. Then the farmer will produce at any cost.
Last fall, after the house closed, the minister made a trip to the west. He said that the growers might expect a much better price for the 1939 crop if the war got no worse or if it should end at any time, and he definitely advised the farmers to increase hog production. He made another trip a little after that, and I have the report of the interview that appeared in the Regina Leader-Post. In large headlines, the statement was attributed to him that the wheat policy announcement might not come until November 1. November 1 was the day the farmer paid his threshing accounts; that was the big day he settled his accounts, and that would be the day on which the government would announce their permanent wheat policy. He must have had in mind this trip overseas. However, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) paid us a visit about that time, and a few days later, in the Regina Leader-Post, there appeared a statement in which that hon. gentleman declared that December 1 would be the big day, and he said he had been advised that the general wheat delivery quota could be fixed for the first week in December. December 1, then, was the big day. I suggest that these two ministers should get together on the announcements they make with respect to this one department of government.
It is quite apparent that the Minister of Agriculture is in more than an advisory capacity. He is head of two other departments, agriculture and national war services, and to a great extent he is manager of public works-he steps in there. If we look over

the situation we find that he is pretty well running about four departments of government. I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that it is time the Minister of Agriculture paid special attention to one department and one only. The producers, he says, must not be pessimistic. Let me say this. In western Canada there is an emergency situation that calls for immediate action. It has come about from one or two causes. I am not going to charge the government with responsibility for the first cause, namely, the loss of a certain amount of the European market where we enjoyed an export trade of 100,000,000 bushels. We have lost that and I am not going to charge the government with responsibility for it; nevertheless that has made the situation more serious. It has become a national problem and one that must be considered as such by this government. It is this government's direct responsibility.
When the war broke out, there were certain problems that were unsolved in Canada. There was the problem of scarcity in the midst of plenty, about which we have heard so much from our friends in the corner to my left; there was the problem of a reasonable standard of living for the Canadian people; there was the problem of parity of prices; and there was the problem of production. These questions are all on the government's doorstep and they have not been courageously dealt with. They must be settled immediately. One cause, then, has been the loss of markets; the other cause is the failure of the government to handle the situation in a constructive, courageous way.
Hon. members will recall that on June 27 last I tried to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing this allimportant public question of wheat, but my effort was frustrated. It was apparent then, however, what was going to happen, and it did happen. I was ruled out of order and nothing was done. Certain bills were rushed through in the last day or two of the session, but no adequate picture was presented to the house.
I contend that we must have action immediately because an emergent situation does exist, a situation that has come about as a result of lack of cash in circulation in western Canada from the crop as compared with what we had in 1939. There is some misunderstanding with respect to farm conditions in the west. We normally market up to the first of November about 75 per cent of the crop. This year by the first of November we had marketed 205,000,000 bushels, whereas last year, on the first of November, we had marketed
312,000,000 bushels. That means, at the same

price

70 cents, netting 50 cents to the farmer -that there was from $50,000,000 to $55,000,000 less in circulation in western Canada on the first of November than there was at the same time last year. The eight-bushel quota, 50 cents, average, pays only current taxes, cost of harvesting and cost of labour. The merchants have not been paid and their position is desperate. Winter is coming on and the farmer has no surplus money to provide fuel or clothing. Things are at a standstill.
I am going to offer a suggestion, because there have been many complaints since last August, since this situation came about, and suggestions have been offered to the government. But see what has happened in Manitoba. The Hon. Mr. Bracken out there has been calling conferences; he has had representatives from all parts of the west meeting with him, and I think he has made suggestions to this government. Evidently they have not listened, and hon. members know what has happened out there. He is going to be down here in a few days, and we had better adjourn pretty soon or he will be here before we get back west.
I have made certain suggestions; the government, while they did not at the time accept them, generally do in the end. Therefore I am offering this one now in the hope that they will act on it, and do so quickly. It is this: to increase the initial price. I want hon. members from western Canada to think it over. They know the situation out there. What more can the government do to relieve this agricultural situation right now? The winter is here. Increase that price to 87i cents, or 90 cents would be better

No, I am not one of those who talk bosh; I am saying what is reasonable. What can this government do to relieve the situation? They can increase this price and make it retroactive to August 1, 1940. That would start about $40,000,000 in circulation at once. But it will all come east. Merchants there are cancelling their wholesale orders, refusing their drafts, but this would start money in circulation. If the government do not do this, they will have to do something which will cost just as much in the end.
In making that suggestion I go further. I am going to show how they can get that and how they can save it. First, on the ordinary expenditure in the next fiscal year they can save at least $30,000,000. They can save under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, if they cut out some of the stuff, at least
$2,000,000. The minister told us last year he was going to cut out $700,000, but he went beyond his authority, he had to stretch it and overspend to the extent of $1,300,000. The government services could be cut so as to save $5,000,000 all over Canada; the overloaded civil service could be reorganized, and $5,000,000 saved there. Then the grain exchange could be closed and we could make a saving there of commissions and brokerage fees paid to that organization for which they are not giving a single dollar's worth; at least $1,000,000 could be saved there. They can save $15,000,000 in storage fees paid on grain now in elevators in western Canada, in these annexes, space offsight as they call it, drawing two-thirds of a cent a bushel a month, and paying for the space in three months. That should be readjusted. Then we should stop paying storage in box cars. And the government should take full charge of the whole grain marketing system in western Canada, including coarse grains and all, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar suggested.
If I had time I could outline how a very great saving could be made to the individual farmer right now. The hon. Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) I venture to say lias heard about it; stop this racket that is being perpetrated on the western farmer this year more than ever before in the last thirty years. Hon. members have been sitting here for thirty years trying to devise a scheme whereby the farmer would get a fair deal in marketing his wheat. We spent a month amending the grain act the last year that Hon. Doctor Motherwell sat in this house. After all that, there was perpetrated this year the greatest racket by way of storage fees, dockages, undergrading and the like, that there ever was. I have samples from the constituency of the Minister of Agriculture; I have sent samples to Ottawa and to the grain inspection at Winnipeg, and have had different grading on the Winnipeg ones-"they have not authority to grade it here"-from that they are giving at the interior elevator. I have in my room samples graded No. 3, and No. 3 rejected; I would like the minister to come and look at them. There is a racket being practised there that should be stopped. There is only one way to do it, that is for this government to have the courage to do it. It is an outrage on the farmers of western Canada to permit it to go on.
Let me now deal with the bankers for a moment. The question of advancing money on wheat on the farm has come up and will come up. If the government did what I suggest, increase the price, with the storage paid to the farmer on the farm, then the
The Address-Mr. Perley

bankers should be told by this government that it is time for them to get into this picture and do their share to relieve that situation by reasonable loans. If the price were around ninety cents and storage paid on the farm at two-thirds of a cent a bushel a month, the bankers should be told to make reasonable advances to the farmers and if they do not, this government should talk to them. The farmer sells his grain to the elevator and the elevator has the power under the grain act to hypothecate the wheat to the bank and get on the wheat the money that he pays to the farmer for it. I would say to the banks, the farmer can hypothecate his wheat in his bin, and you make these advances, or we will take steps to see that you do, or do something with respect to amending the Canadian Bank Act.	The
government can do a lot of things if only they have the courage.
Suggestions have been made with respect to stopping the importation into Canada of agricultural products; pork products were instanced by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon).
Then I would refer for a moment to domestic freight rates. The government can do a great deal for the farmers by readjusting those rates; this pork production means that our coarse grains should be coming east in greater quantities, as they would if the freight rates were adjusted.
My time is almost up. I appeal to this government to take action immediately along the lines I have suggested. By doing so they would give a measure of justice to the farmers of western Canada. We are all behind the government in doing anything at all to put this industry in its proper place. The farmers are patriotic; let us deal with them in such a way that they can go hand in hand with us; the effort that Canada is putting forth at the present time will be of such a character that we shall emerge with democracy saved, and liberty and justice preserved, and we shall be first in the great commonwealth of British dominions. The Canadian farmers will do their part.

I refer specifically to the statement reported to have been made by the leader of the opposition, in which he said that the Ogdensburg meeting between the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) of Canada and the President of the United States was made in part with the idea of ensuring the president's reelection. If such a speech were made, I believe that the best interests of the British empire were not served.
I believe that any speech or word that tends to weaken friendly relations which exist between the British empire and other democracies is dangerous and unpatriotic.
It is further reported that in the same speech the leader of the opposition stated he was not unaware of the attitude in the past of our Prime Minister toward the United States. I am glad the leader of the opposition is aware of the attitude of our Prime Minister toward the people of the United States. I hope that all hon. members are aware of that attitude. I hope that that attitude is made clear to every Canadian citizen from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I will go farther. I wish that attitude could be .made clear to all the nations of the world. It has been one of friendliness and cooperation, and had it been followed by the nations of Europe we would not now be embroiled in this most beastly and horrible war. If the attitude of our Prime Minister has resulted in nothing more than a cementing of the friendship between the United States and the British empire, then it is my considered opinion that he has done more than any other living man for the British empire.
Among the criticisms levelled at the government mention has been made of the inefficiency of the government's mobilization act which was passed at the last session of parliament. Criticism of this kind is puerile and discloses a lack of understanding of its purpose and its effect. Allow me by comparison with the Military Service Act of 1917 to indicate the difference in effect of the two acts upon Canada as a nation. The Military Service Act of 1917, adopted by the then union government, actually disunited this country, while the effect of the mobilization act of 1940 is consistent with the government's policy of building and maintaining a united Canada.
The whole country from the Atlantic to the Pacific is responding nobly because of its realization that the mobilization act of 1940 has been passed with one object in view, namely the training and preparation of our man-power. It has been designed for our selfpreservation and for the preservation of our democratic institutions.

By way of further
criticism we have heard it said that our factories are not yet producing rifles, ammunition. uniforms, boots and other equipment required by our troops. I would place this unwarranted criticism under the heading of either lack of information or the desire to misinform.
With respect to the production of guns in Canadian factories I received a bulletin on October 17 stating that we in Canada were about to produce some of the largest naval guns produced in the British empire. That statement was reported to have been made by a minister. On October 21 a correction came to me saying that the minister had stated that naval guns were shortly to be produced in Canada in a factory which was one of the largest in the British empire.
I respectfully suggest that a copy of this correction should be mailed to the leader of the opposition, because apparently his copy has gone astray. I recall clearly that during the last world war the training of the third Canadian division artillery in Canada was accomplished without any weapons whatsoever. In fact we did not touch a piece of field artillery until we reached England, and only two and a half months before we landed in France on active service. Our complete training in Canada consisted of adapting ourselves to military discipline and getting ourselves in good physical condition. Notwithstanding this, the division wrote history by their loyalty and valour. Canadian troops seemed to adapt themselves to any position in which they found themselves in the last war, and I have every confidence that that old tradition will be lived up to by the present army. So we see just how unwarranted criticism of the kind I have indicated may be, when we realize that within fourteen months of our entering the war we are operating on a colossal war-producing basis. We are producing practically all the instruments of war, to say nothing of the fact that we are making Canada the hub of the empire's training scheme.
May I respectfully add my plea to that which has been made by other hon. members respecting the proposal that the government

I think all hon. members are well aware of the importance of home ties to our men who are proceeding overseas. I feel I would be lacking in my duty if I did not add my voice to those already raised in asking the government to give this matter their earnest attention.
There is another matter which has not been brought up by any previous speaker and which, I believe, is quite praiseworthy. I refer to the evacuees from Europe and the British isles who have been coming to Canada. The humanitarian efforts which have been put forth by the government and the civil service are most praiseworthy, and I should like to add my congratulations to the government upon making this possible. As I go through my riding of Mount Royal daily, I meet many evacuees, and they are all pleased to be in the country and most thankful that they have been given a haven of refuge.
This brings up another matter, the increase in industry which has taken place because of this evacuee movement. I would mention the Bata shoe company which was brought to Canada by men of capital in Czechoslovakia. I cannot give the exact statistics, but I know that several other industries have located in this country and are now giving employment to thousands of Canadians. Industries have been set up where there were no industries before, and all this is the direct result of the splendid efforts put forward by our government to take care of these refugees from Europe. This dominion is growing and it will continue to grow. Never in its history have commercial and industrial strides been so great as those which have occurred in the last twelve months. I think the Prime Minister and the government are
be congratulated upon having facilitated this movement.
We see that things are going along fairly evenly at this critical time. Futile and vicious criticism does not help our war effort, nor does it tend toward unity. At this time unity in Canada is of paramount importance.
I know that all members of the opposition will agree that even though it may not serve the best interests of their parties, it would
[Mr. Whitman.l
be morally wrong for them not to accept the dictum that unity for Canada should be the watchword to-day. If it would be morally wrong for them not to accept that dictum, then it cannot be politically right. The great Irish statesman Daniel O'Connell said that nothing is politically right that is morally wrong. This is the time of sacrifice, political and otherwise. Unity must prevail. Nothing must be done by any individual or group of individuals that will interfere in the minutest degree with our struggle for selfpreservation. Nothing would be more dangerous than unwholesome or thoughtless criticism, or the throwing of questions at the government with 'the single object of embarrassing them.
Let us all be mindful of the philosophy of the well-known -philosopher who said that a few drops of oil will set the political machine in motion, whereas a ton of vinegar will only corrode and canker. Let us keep oiling the machine and see that no one attempts to corrode and canker our war effort. This is the time for extreme trust, collaboration and unity. It is not a time for mistrust, prejudice and disruption. No finer words have been uttered than those uttered on the floor of this house by no less a personage than that great Liberal leader and philosopher, the late Sir Wilfrid La-urier, who said: "Love is better than hate, truth is better than falsehood, trust is better than suspicion."
